personalEssay.prompt: Describe a topic, idea, or concept you find so engaging that it makes you lose all track of time. Why does it captivate you? What or who do you turn to when you want to learn more?
personalEssay.text:
Here is a question that ruined my summer, in the best way: why does every prime number bigger than three sit right next to a multiple of six?

Try it. Five and seven sit on either side of six. Eleven and thirteen, either side of twelve. Seventeen and nineteen, eighteen. Twenty-three, twenty-four. It keeps going. When I first noticed this in ninth grade, during a very boring study hall, I thought I had discovered something huge. I wrote it on my hand and showed my math teacher. She smiled, the kind of smile that means you're about to learn something humbling, and showed me why it has to be true. Any whole number is either a multiple of six, or one, two, three, four, or five more than one. If it's two or four more, it's even. If it's three more, it's divisible by three. That only leaves one more and five more, which are the neighbors of a multiple of six.

I was a little disappointed it wasn't a new discovery. But I was much more amazed that it could be proved. Not checked a thousand times. Proved, forever, in four lines.

That was the beginning. Since then I've lost more hours than I can count to number theory, the part of math that studies whole numbers. On the surface it seems like the simplest subject there is. You learned the numbers when you were three. But underneath, it's full of questions so hard that nobody has solved them in hundreds of years. Are there infinitely many twin primes, pairs like eleven and thirteen? Nobody knows. A kid in a study hall can ask a question that the best mathematicians in the world can't answer. I think that's beautiful.

Last summer, I spent eight weeks at the Ross Mathematics Program at Ohio State. Ross is famous for its motto, "Think deeply of simple things," and for giving you problem sets that seem easy and turn out to take three days. Every morning we got a new set of problems, and every afternoon I sat in the lounge and got stuck. Really stuck. Some days I didn't solve a single problem. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, harder than any soccer practice, and I'd do it again tomorrow.

The weirdest part was that Ross was twenty minutes from my house. My mom drove me there with three suitcases of food, like I was moving across the world, and then I lived in a dorm for the first time with students from fifteen different countries. Sometimes on weekends my little sisters would come visit and I'd show them the problems on the whiteboard. They didn't understand any of it, but they liked the colored markers.

Math also changed how I see the rest of my life. I translate a lot for my parents, who came from Addis Ababa when I was four. At the doctor, at the bank, at parent-teacher conferences. Translation is like proof in a way. You're trying to find a path from one language to another without losing anything true. Sometimes there's no direct path, and you have to go around.

Even soccer is a little bit math. As a striker, I'm always calculating angles and spaces, where the defender will be in two seconds, where the gap opens. My coach doesn't call it geometry, but it is.

When I want to learn more, I read. Right now I'm working through an old number theory textbook my Ross counselor recommended, one chapter a week. I watch lectures online. I email my old Ross counselors with questions, and they actually answer.

I still don't know why twin primes keep showing up. Nobody does. But I've learned that not knowing is where math starts.

supplements.prompt: Please tell us what you are interested in studying at college and why.
supplements.text:
I want to study mathematics, specifically number theory, and I want to understand how pure math connects to the real world.

My interest started with a pattern I noticed in ninth grade: every prime number bigger than three sits next to a multiple of six. My teacher showed me how to prove it, and I've been hooked on proofs ever since. Last summer, at the Ross Mathematics Program, I spent weeks working on problems that seemed simple but took days to solve. I loved being stuck. I loved the moment something finally clicked.

But I'm also interested in how math gets used. Number theory used to be considered the most useless branch of math, and now it's the foundation of modern cryptography. Every time you buy something online, prime numbers are protecting your information. I find it amazing that ideas people studied just for their beauty ended up being so important.

At WashU, I'd want to major in mathematics and possibly minor in computer science, so I can explore cryptography and security. I'm excited about doing undergraduate research with faculty and joining the math club. I'd also love to tutor younger students, like I do at the library now, because explaining math to a nine-year-old is one of the best ways to understand it yourself.

I also translate for my family, and I think there's a connection between translation and proof. Both are about finding a path from one place to another without losing what's true. I want to keep finding those paths in college.
